A reward model scores a response to a prompt with one number, and in RLHF, a policy is then trained to make that number large.
The reward model only saw a finite set of comparisons, though, and the policy is free to wander off to responses that look like none of them.
There, the reward is an extrapolation, and a policy that maximizes it can find responses that the reward model scores highly but people wouldn't.
This is reward-model overoptimization (Gao et al., 2023)[^gao2023].
Yang et al. (2024)[^yang2024rm] put a Laplace approximation on the reward model, so that every reward comes with a variance.
They then penalize the rewards that the model is unsure about.

On this page, we fit a Laplace approximation to a published reward model and ask whether its reward variance is larger on prompts and responses unlike the ones it was trained on.

## Bradley–Terry and the Laplace approximation

Let $r_\theta(x)$ be the reward of a text $x$, a prompt together with a response.
A preference pair is two responses $a$ and $b$ to the same prompt, with $a$ the one a person preferred.
The Bradley–Terry model (1952)[^bradley1952] says this happens with probability

$$
  p(a \succ b \mid \theta) = \sigma\big(r_\theta(a) - r_\theta(b)\big) ,
$$

with $\sigma$ the logistic sigmoid.
That is the softmax over the two rewards.
So `lk.reward.bradley_terry()` is a categorical likelihood over the pair's two rewards, with the label $0$ for "the first one won".
Only the difference of the rewards enters, so adding a constant to every reward changes nothing.

With $N$ pairs and $\theta_*$ the trained weights, the Laplace approximation is

$$
  p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \approx \mathcal{N}(\theta \mid \theta_*, \Sigma) , \qquad \Sigma^{-1} = \lambda I + \sum_{i=1}^N J_i^\top H_i J_i ,
$$

where $J_i$ is the $2 \times P$ Jacobian of the two rewards of pair $i$ and $H_i$ the Hessian of $-\log p$ with respect to them.
With $p_i = \sigma(r(a_i) - r(b_i))$ and $u = (1, -1)^\top$, it is $H_i = p_i (1 - p_i) \, u u^\top$, so

$$
  J_i^\top H_i J_i = p_i (1 - p_i) \, \big(\nabla_\theta r(a_i) - \nabla_\theta r(b_i)\big) \big(\nabla_\theta r(a_i) - \nabla_\theta r(b_i)\big)^\top .
$$

With this exact GGN, the data add curvature only along the differences of the reward gradients.
A direction that moves all rewards together, such as the bias of the last layer, gets none, and its variance stays at the prior's.
This is the idealized picture, and the KFAC fit below departs from it.

Linearizing $r_\theta$ around $\theta_*$ gives each text a Gaussian reward, with mean $r_{\theta_*}(x)$ and variance

$$
  v(x) = \nabla_\theta r(x)^\top \, \Sigma \, \nabla_\theta r(x) .
$$

$v(x)$ is small when the gradient at $x$ points along directions that the preference data pinned down.
Otherwise, it grows toward the prior's $\|\nabla_\theta r(x)\|^2 / \lambda$.
Yang et al. use it through a penalized reward, e.g.,

$$
  \tilde r(x) = r_{\theta_*}(x) - k \sqrt{v(x)} ,
$$

with some $k > 0$.
Where the reward model extrapolates, the hope is that $v(x)$ is large.
The penalty then takes back the reward that the model can't vouch for, and the policy gains less from going there.

The [Quickstart](../quickstart/reward.py) does all this on a toy problem with three input features, where the reward's standard deviation grows past the range of the data.
Here we use a real reward model.

::: {#cb48347f .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import warnings

import datasets
import huggingface_hub
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import transformers
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

import laplacekit as lk

transformers.logging.set_verbosity_error()
transformers.utils.logging.disable_progress_bar()
datasets.disable_progress_bars()
huggingface_hub.logging.set_verbosity_error()
warnings.filterwarnings(
    "ignore", category=FutureWarning
)  # deprecation notices from transformers
```
:::


## Model and data

The model is `nicholasKluge/RewardModel`[^aira] on the Hugging Face Hub, pinned to one revision.
It is a BERT-base sequence classifier with 108 million parameters and one output, the reward.
It reads the prompt and the response as a BERT sentence pair.
We load it with eager attention, as on the [Language models](llm.py) page.

::: {#63c589c1 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
MODEL = "nicholasKluge/RewardModel"
MODEL_REV = "914413962bfc33b1b703942b2920bd1b7b6e3b27"
DATA_REV = (
    "ecfeb1936069f37bee7daffee60cd7765c326a34"  # the data as of August 2023
)

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL, revision=MODEL_REV)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    MODEL, revision=MODEL_REV, attn_implementation="eager"
)
_ = model.eval()

aira = load_dataset(
    "nicholasKluge/reward-aira-dataset", revision=DATA_REV, split="english"
)
print(aira)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Dataset({
    features: ['instruction', 'chosen_response', 'rejected_response'],
    num_rows: 32675
})
```
:::
:::


The model was trained on the English part of `reward-aira-dataset`.
Its English data was replaced in January 2024.
So we pin the version that was on the Hub when the model was uploaded, in August 2023: 32,675 prompts, each with a chosen and a rejected response.
We fit the Laplace approximation on the first 32 pairs, in four batches of eight.

`prepare_preferences` takes each batch as a dictionary with the tokenizer output of the chosen responses under `"chosen"` and that of the rejected ones under `"rejected"`.
The two sides must have the same length, so we tokenize them in one padded call and split the result.
Many responses are long, and we cut each pair at 128 tokens to keep the fit fast on a CPU.

::: {#b15bc997 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def preferences(rows):
    n = len(rows)
    both = tok(
        list(rows["instruction"]) * 2,
        list(rows["chosen_response"]) + list(rows["rejected_response"]),
        padding=True,
        truncation=True,
        max_length=128,
        return_tensors="pt",
    )

    return {
        "chosen": {k: v[:n] for k, v in both.items()},
        "rejected": {k: v[n:] for k, v in both.items()},
    }


batches = [preferences(aira.select(range(i, i + 8))) for i in range(0, 32, 8)]
```
:::


## Fitting the last layer

`lk.transformers.sequence_classification` makes the model return its output.
`lk.reward.pairwise` turns the result into a model that scores both sides of a pair in one forward pass.
We put the Laplace approximation on the weight of the last layer, `classifier.weight`, i.e., the 768 numbers that map BERT's pooled features to the reward.
We leave out its bias, which is a shift of all rewards that the likelihood can't see.
The curvature is KFAC, as in Laplace-LoRA (Yang et al., 2024)[^yang2024lora].
`DenseGGN` would keep the exact GGN from above, but it needs `vmap`, which the probe doesn't find for this BERT.

`pairwise` runs both sides of a pair through the model as one batch, and KFAC treats the two texts as separate examples.
Its input factor is the second moment of each text's own features, without the cross terms between the two sides.
So it adds curvature along each text's features, not only along the differences.
A shift of all rewards then gets curvature too: under KFAC, even a bias would end up with a variance below the prior's.
Thus, $v(x)$ here measures how far the features of $x$ stray from those of the 64 texts in the fit, more than how far its gradient strays from the directions that the preferences pin down.

The 32 pairs give the average curvature, and `n_data=len(aira)` scales it to $N = 32{,}675$.
The marginal likelihood picks $\lambda$.

::: {#90ef1d8f .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fn = lk.reward.pairwise(lk.transformers.sequence_classification(model))
data = lk.data.from_loader(
    batches, prepare=lk.reward.prepare_preferences, n_data=len(aira)
)

post = lk.laplace(
    fn,
    data,
    likelihood=lk.reward.bradley_terry(),
    subset=lk.subsets.named("classifier.weight"),
    hessian_approx=lk.KFAC(),
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
)
print(post)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
LaplacePosterior(
  subset         = named {"classifier.weight": (1, 768)}
  hessian_approx = KFAC()
  curvature      = BlockDiag[KronEigenbasis] (1 block, 768 parameters)
  prior          = Isotropic(prior_precision=84.8)
  likelihood     = Categorical()
  hyper_tuner    = MarginalLikelihood()
  n_data         = 32675
)
```
:::
:::


The marginal likelihood chose $\lambda \approx 85$.

::: {.callout-note}
For Laplace-LoRA on a reward model, the model is a `peft` model with LoRA adapters and a trainable score head, and the call is the same with `subset=lk.subsets.trainable`.
:::

## Rewards and their variance

We compare two groups of four texts.
The first group has prompts with their chosen responses from the same version of the dataset, but not among the 32 pairs.
They are the first four of rows 32 to 1,999 whose prompt and response together fit in 64 tokens.
The second group has prompts and responses unlike the training data (OOD): German, keyboard noise, SQL and Japanese.
Our OOD texts are short, so we keep the first group short too, so that the length doesn't differ between the groups.
Each group is padded to its longest text, and `lk.predict_outputs` gives the reward of each text with its variance.
Without `vmap`, the variance comes from 64 sampled draws, so we seed them with a generator.

::: {#988bbc95 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
held = aira.select(range(32, 2000))
lengths = [
    len(ids)
    for ids in tok(list(held["instruction"]), list(held["chosen_response"]))[
        "input_ids"
    ]
]
short = held.select([i for i, n in enumerate(lengths) if n <= 64][:4])

groups = {
    "in": list(
        zip(short["instruction"], short["chosen_response"], strict=True)
    ),
    "OOD": [
        ("Wie spät ist es?", "Es ist drei Uhr."),
        ("asdf qwer zxcv", "1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9"),
        ("Write a SQL query that lists all users.", "SELECT * FROM users;"),
        ("Translate 'cat' into Japanese.", "猫 (neko)"),
    ],
}

rewards = {}

for name, texts in groups.items():
    x = tok(
        [p for p, _ in texts],
        [r for _, r in texts],
        padding=True,
        return_tensors="pt",
    )
    out = lk.predict_outputs(
        post, x, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    )
    rewards[name] = (
        out.mean.squeeze(-1),
        out.cov.per_input().reshape(-1).sqrt(),
    )

print(f"{'':<4} {'reward':>7} {'std':>6}  prompt")

for name, texts in groups.items():
    for (prompt, _), r, s in zip(texts, *rewards[name], strict=True):
        print(
            f"{name:<4} {float(r):7.2f} {float(s):6.3f}  "
            f"{prompt.splitlines()[0][:48]}"
        )

for name, (_, s) in rewards.items():
    print(f"mean std, {name}: {float(s.mean()):.3f}")
```

The four chosen responses get rewards from 6.67 to 11.91, and the OOD texts from -8.21 to -1.45.
The OOD texts also get a larger standard deviation on average, 0.517 against 0.321.
But the ranges overlap: 0.409 to 0.570 for the OOD texts, and 0.127 to 0.445 for the others.
The SQL query, at 0.409, is less uncertain than the question about pronouncing "architecture", at 0.445.
The largest standard deviation of all, 0.570, goes to the Japanese translation, which is also the OOD text with the highest reward.

Next, we plot each text's standard deviation against its reward, for both groups together.

::: {#26b24db7 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r_all = torch.cat([r for r, _ in rewards.values()])
s_all = torch.cat([s for _, s in rewards.values()])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))

for name, (r, s) in rewards.items():
    ax.scatter(r, s, label=name)

ax.set_xlabel("reward")
ax.set_ylabel("std of the reward")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

print(
    "correlation of reward and std: "
    f"{float(torch.corrcoef(torch.stack([r_all, s_all]))[0, 1]):.2f}"
)
```

Over the eight texts, the correlation of reward and standard deviation is -0.74.
It comes mostly from the split between the groups: the chosen responses have high rewards and smaller standard deviations, and the OOD texts low rewards and larger ones.
Within the OOD group, the order goes the other way, since the Japanese text has both the highest reward and the largest standard deviation.
With four texts per group, neither pattern is pinned down.

For the penalized reward $\tilde r$, the Japanese text is the interesting case.
It is an unusual text that scores higher than the other OOD texts, and its penalty is the largest of the eight.
Its reward is still far below those of the chosen responses, though.
So this page doesn't show what the variance does for an unusual text that the model scores as highly as a good response, which is the case that matters most for overoptimization.

## Wrap-up

A published reward model gets a Laplace approximation in one `lk.laplace` call.
`lk.reward.pairwise` scores both sides of a pair, `prepare_preferences` turns tokenized chosen and rejected responses into a batch, and `bradley_terry()` is the likelihood.
`lk.predict_outputs` then gives every text's reward with its variance.
On this BERT reward model, with Laplace on the 768 weights of its last layer, four OOD texts get a larger reward standard deviation on average than four chosen responses from the training data.
The groups overlap, and the OOD text with the highest reward has the largest standard deviation.
Yang et al. put the Laplace approximation on LoRA adapters throughout the network, which `subset=lk.subsets.trainable` gives on a `peft` model.
